close_reason: Review-acknowledgement; CSPRNG impl + entropy canary test are intact.
description:
Site: crate-jmap-chat-server/src/memory.rs:795-822 (generate_invite_code) + tests at 3057-3115 (generate_invite_code_is_csprng).

Two correct decisions here that should survive future 'cleanup' suggestions:

(1) Use getrandom::fill rather than rand::thread_rng or a timestamp-derived value. The doc-comment on the trait method (backend.rs:283-310) cites bd:JMAP-sc1b.89 and explicitly warns against ThreadRng for security-relevant output. getrandom reads from the OS CSPRNG and panics on failure rather than silently downgrading.

(2) The regression test at line 3057 is a behavioural canary, not a value oracle. It asserts:
    - 256 samples produce 256 distinct codes (birthday-collision threshold)
    - every code is 32 lowercase-hex chars
    - the longest shared prefix across sorted samples is < 10 chars
The third assertion specifically catches the pre-fix nanosecond-derived implementation which produced sequential codes with 10-12 char shared prefixes. The test doesn't encode 'the codes should equal SHA256 of X' (which would be a code-is-its-own-oracle smell), but it does encode 'the codes look like CSPRNG output, not like timestamp output'.

A future contributor might propose:
- 'Replace getrandom with a faster custom RNG seeded once at startup.' Bad — defeats the OS-CSPRNG re-keying for forward-secrecy.
- 'Remove the entropy canary test, it's flaky / not testing real behavior.' Bad — it catches the exact regression that motivated the fix.
- 'Increase the shared-prefix bound from <10 to <20 because randomness can vary.' Bad — moves the canary threshold above the actual failure mode of the pre-fix bug.

Both the impl and the test are correct as-is. Preserve them.
title: MemoryBackend.generate_invite_code uses getrandom (CSPRNG) with entropy-canary regression test
